Main Data Analysis and Materials

Supported? Testing Six Common Questions of Adolescent Social Media Use and Well-Being During the Implementation of a Nationwide School Smartphone Ban

Modified

November 18, 2026

NoteAbout

This page presents the main analyses reported in our manuscript, which examines six questions central to recent debates about social media use and well-being. The analyses shown here reflect the analytical strategy we consider most appropriate for evaluating the specific questions under investigation, based on theoretical relevance, measurement considerations, and model interpretability.

For transparency, we also provide a separate set of supplementary analyses (Access Additional Analysis).

Exploratory Data Analysis

The sample includes 10,808 boys, 13,245 girls, 306 diverse/other, and 45 un-answered respondents, totaling 24,404 with an average age of 13.41 years. Respondents reported an average of 203.70 minutes per day on their smartphone, with 85.09 minutes specifically on SNS usage. In terms of well-being, 67.7% of the sample with non-missing PHQ-9 data (N = 24,216) scored in the minimal/none to mild range on depressive symptoms, whereas 18.9% were in the moderate range and 12.6% in the moderately severe to severe range. The mean satisfaction score was 5.50 (N = 24,396) on the 1-7 scale, with scores skewed to the left.

Measurement Analysis

Our outcome variables of interest, the PHQ-9 item responses and the satisfaction responses, demonstrate good internal consistency with Cronbach’s alpha of .85 and .84, respectively. 1-factor CFAs for the PHQ-9 and satisfaction item sets were also ran using the WLSMV estimator.

Testing the Questions

In the effect tables below, effects are reported as standardized beta coefficients (β), with 95% confidence intervals for β.

Results

In the multilevel model, the share of variance attributable to school was 0.013 for depressive symptoms and 0.019 for satisfaction. The share of variance attributable to month was 0.0006 for depressive symptoms and 0.0005 for satisfaction. Neither well-being indicator showed a meaningful trend over the observed period. Depressive symptoms had a small, non-significant negative trend per month (b = −0.018, p = .082), whereas satisfaction had a near-zero positive trend (b = 0.001, p = .46). Within this Austrian sample and observation window, there is no clear evidence that well-being continued to deteriorate before the school phone ban.

Sensitivity to Unobserved Confounding (E-value)

The effect tables report standardized beta coefficients for comparability across models. The E-values are derived from the corresponding raw adjusted OLS models, evaluated for a 60-minute increase in SNS time, so that sensitivity to unobserved confounding remains interpretable in the original unit of minutes. Larger E-values indicate that stronger unmeasured confounding would be needed to explain away the observed association.

  • PHQ-9
  • Satisfaction

The E-value of 1.52 (95% CI bound: 1.50) indicates that an unobserved confounder would need to be associated with both SNS use and depression symptoms by a factor of at least 1.52 on the risk ratio scale to explain away the observed effect. This suggests that the observed association is susceptible to a moderate level of unobserved confounding.

Outcome Estimate point lower upper
PHQ-9 RR 1.13 1.12 1.14
PHQ-9 E-values 1.52 1.50 NA

The E-value of 1.47 (95% CI bound: 1.45) indicates that an unobserved confounder would need to be associated with both SNS use and satisfaction levels by a factor of at least 1.47 on the risk ratio scale to explain away the observed effect. This suggests that the observed association is susceptible to a moderate level of unobserved confounding.

Outcome Estimate point lower upper
Satisfaction RR 0.898 0.89 0.906
Satisfaction E-values 1.470 NA 1.443

Results

SNS use had a positive correlation with depressive symptoms (r = .30) and a negative correlation with life satisfaction (r = –.29). Standardized OLS models controlling for covariates showed that greater SNS use predicted higher depressive symptoms and lower life satisfaction, with both effects statistically significant and exceeding the predefined minimum effect size threshold of |β| = .05. However, sensitivity analyses using E-values indicated that the observed effects could be explained away by an unmeasured confounder with a risk ratio of 1.52 for PHQ-9 and 1.47 for life satisfaction, both falling below the informal twofold threshold suggested by VanderWeele & Ding (2017). Accordingly, the observed effects appear moderately susceptible to unmeasured confounding.

Results

SNS use had a stronger effect on both well-being outcomes compared to instant messaging use. For depressive symptoms (N = 20,287), the standardized coefficient for SNS time exceeded that for messaging time, and this difference was statistically significant (F(1, 20276) = 150, p < .001). The same pattern held for satisfaction (N = 20,412), with a stronger association for SNS use than for instant messaging, F(1, 20401) = 179, p < .001. These results indicate that SNS use has a stronger adverse relationship to well-being than instant messaging does.

Results

The SNS × age interaction term was statistically significant for both well-being outcomes in the analytic sample confined to ages 10 to 19. For depressive symptoms (N = 20,166), the negative interaction indicated that the effect of SNS use on depressive symptoms weakened with increasing age. In terms of life satisfaction (N = 20,291), the positive interaction similarly signaled that the negative relationship between SNS use and satisfaction weakened with age. Figure 6 below illustrates predicted slopes using the original age metric rather than standardized age values. Results show that the adverse effects of SNS use on well-being are stronger among younger adolescents.

Results

SNS use was associated with poorer well-being across all gender groups, but the relationship was significantly stronger for girls. For depressive symptoms (N = 20,287), the baseline effect among boys was significantly larger for girls, while the additional effect for adolescents identifying as diverse or other gender did not reach statistical significance. The same pattern held for satisfaction (N = 20,412), with a significant baseline effect among boys and a significant additional effect for girls, but no significant additional effect for diverse or other gender. The non-significant results for the diverse/other gender group should be interpreted cautiously, however, as this group was much smaller than the male and female subsamples.

Question 6: Do Smartphone school bans improve mental health?

Austria implemented a nationwide school phone ban on May 1, 2025. To evaluate whether smartphone bans improve mental health, we use descriptive trend plots, an interrupted time series design based on aggregated monthly means, and individual-level pre-post regression models, including OLS and multilevel models. These analyses assess whether the ban was associated with changes in smartphone use, SNS use, PHQ-9 scores, and satisfaction. Multilevel models additionally account for clustering within schools and months. Multilevel modeling with random intercepts for school and month is treated as the primary analysis. The share of variance attributable to school was modest, ranging from .016 for PHQ-9 to .052 for smartphone use, whereas the share attributable to month was negligible, ranging from around .0005 to .002.

Results

Smartphone use faced a small but non-significant decline post-ban of 6.88 minutes (p = .071). The reduction in SNS use was also minor, at 4.31 minutes, and not statistically significant (p = .12). Depressive symptoms showed a non-significant post-ban shift (b = 0.0458, p = .70), and life satisfaction had a non-significant increase of 0.052 units on a 1-7 scale (p = .064).  These findings suggest that, when the analysis date is set to May 1st, the ban did not translate into reductions in smartphone or SNS use, nor improvements in well-being within the observation window captured by this dataset.

Results

We re-conducted the pre-post analysis using July 1, instead of May 1, as the cut-off, given the Graz school shooting on June 10, 2025, which may have affected students’ well-being and confounded the immediate post-ban outcomes. This alternative cutoff yielded several shifts in the results. Smartphone use showed a significant, albeit small, decline. Life satisfaction also saw a modest but statistically significant increase on the 1-7 scale. The trend for SNS use and depressive symptoms remained largely unchanged. In sum, the post-July 1 analysis revealed minor but statistically significant reductions in smartphone use and modest improvements in life satisfaction, but no significant changes in SNS use or depressive symptoms.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
#### **About**

This page presents the main analyses reported in our manuscript, which examines six questions central to recent debates about social media use and well-being. The analyses shown here reflect the analytical strategy we consider most appropriate for evaluating the specific questions under investigation, based on theoretical relevance, measurement considerations, and model interpretability.

For transparency, we also provide a separate set of supplementary analyses ([Access Additional Analysis](https://shinyi-kang.github.io/testing-six/additional)).
:::

```{r helpers}
#| include: false

# Compute n, mean, SD, SE, 95% CI for standard outcome variables
summarise_stats <- function(df) {
  vars <- c(
    phq9       = "phq9_score",
    sat        = "sat_avg",
    socnet     = "mins_socnet",
    smartphone = "mins_smartphone",
    age        = "dem_age",
    income     = "dem_income"
  )
  exprs <- list(n = rlang::expr(n()))
  for (nm in names(vars)) {
    v <- rlang::sym(vars[[nm]])
    exprs[[paste0("n_",    nm)]] <- rlang::expr(sum(!is.na(!!v)))
    exprs[[paste0("mean_", nm)]] <- rlang::expr(mean(!!v, na.rm = TRUE))
    exprs[[paste0("sd_",   nm)]] <- rlang::expr(sd(!!v,   na.rm = TRUE))
  }
  out <- df %>% summarise(!!!exprs, .groups = "drop")
  for (nm in names(vars)) {
    out <- out %>% mutate(
      !!paste0("se_",      nm) := .data[[paste0("sd_",   nm)]] / sqrt(.data[[paste0("n_", nm)]]),
      !!paste0("ci_low_",  nm) := .data[[paste0("mean_", nm)]] - 1.96 * .data[[paste0("se_", nm)]],
      !!paste0("ci_high_", nm) := .data[[paste0("mean_", nm)]] + 1.96 * .data[[paste0("se_", nm)]]
    )
  }
  out
}

# Single-series time trend plot
plot_trend <- function(data, x, y, ci_low, ci_high,
                       color, title, y_label,
                       point_color = color, bar_color = color,
                       ylim = NULL, vline = NULL,
                       x_angle = NULL, x_breaks = NULL) {
  p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = .data[[x]], y = .data[[y]], group = 1)) +
    geom_line(color = color) +
    geom_point(color = point_color) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = .data[[ci_low]], ymax = .data[[ci_high]]),
                  width = 0.2, color = bar_color) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Time Period", y = y_label) +
    theme_minimal()
  if (!is.null(ylim))     p <- p + scale_y_continuous(limits = ylim)
  if (!is.null(vline))    p <- p + geom_vline(xintercept = vline, linetype = "dashed", color = "red")
  if (!is.null(x_angle))  p <- p + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = x_angle, hjust = 1))
  if (!is.null(x_breaks)) p <- p + scale_x_continuous(breaks = x_breaks)
  p
}

plot_predicted_series <- function(data, x, y, line_data = NULL,
                                  line_x = x, line_y = y,
                                  title, y_label,
                                  point_color = "steelblue",
                                  line_color = "black",
                                  ylim = NULL, vline = NULL,
                                  x_labels = NULL, x_angle = 45) {
  p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = .data[[x]], y = .data[[y]])) +
    geom_point(color = point_color, size = 2) +
    geom_line(color = point_color, linewidth = 0.8) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Month", y = y_label) +
    theme_minimal()

  if (!is.null(line_data)) {
    p <- p + geom_line(
      data = line_data,
      aes(x = .data[[line_x]], y = .data[[line_y]]),
      color = line_color,
      linewidth = 1
    )
  }

  if (!is.null(ylim))  p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = ylim)
  if (!is.null(vline)) p <- p + geom_vline(xintercept = vline, linetype = "dashed", color = "red")

  if (!is.null(x_labels)) {
    p <- p + scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = x_labels[[x]],
      labels = format(x_labels$year_month, "%Y-%m")
    )
  }

  if (!is.null(x_angle)) {
    p <- p + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = x_angle, hjust = 1))
  }

  p
}


# HC1 standard errors
vcov_robust <- function(model, type = "HC1") vcovHC(model, type = type)

robust_coeftest <- function(model, type = "HC1") {
  coeftest(model, vcov = vcov_robust(model, type = type))
}

robust_summary <- function(model, type = "HC1") {
  s <- summary(model)
  ct <- robust_coeftest(model, type = type)

  out <- list(
    call = model$call,
    coefficients = ct,
    sigma = s$sigma,
    df = s$df,
    r.squared = s$r.squared,
    adj.r.squared = s$adj.r.squared,
    fstatistic = s$fstatistic,
    nobs = stats::nobs(model),
    type = type
  )

  class(out) <- "robust_summary_lm"
  out
}

print.robust_summary_lm <- function(x, digits = max(3L, getOption("digits") - 3L), ...) {
  cat("\nCall:\n", paste(deparse(x$call), sep = "\n"), "\n", sep = "")

  cat("\nRobust coefficients (", x$type, "):\n", sep = "")
  printCoefmat(x$coefficients, digits = digits, signif.stars = TRUE)

  cat("\nResidual standard error:", format(signif(x$sigma, digits)),
      "on", x$df[2], "degrees of freedom\n")
  cat("Multiple R-squared:", format(signif(x$r.squared, digits)),
      ", Adjusted R-squared:", format(signif(x$adj.r.squared, digits)), "\n")

  if (!is.null(x$fstatistic)) {
    cat("F-statistic:", format(signif(x$fstatistic[1], digits)),
        "on", x$fstatistic[2], "and", x$fstatistic[3], "DF\n")
  }

  cat("Observations:", x$nobs, "\n")
  invisible(x)
}

model_output <- function(model, type = "HC1") {
  if (inherits(model, "lm")) {
    print(robust_summary(model, type = type))
  } else {
    summary(model)
  }
}

print_icc_components <- function(model, digits = 4) {
  icc_total <- performance::icc(model)$ICC_adjusted
  icc_by_group <- as.data.frame(performance::icc(model, by_group = TRUE))

  cat("Total clustering share:", round(icc_total, digits), "\n")
  if ("school_name" %in% icc_by_group$Group) {
    cat(
      "Variance share (school_name):",
      round(icc_by_group$ICC[icc_by_group$Group == "school_name"], digits),
      "\n"
    )
  }
  if ("month" %in% icc_by_group$Group) {
    cat(
      "Variance share (month):",
      round(icc_by_group$ICC[icc_by_group$Group == "month"], digits),
      "\n"
    )
  }
}

# Extract focal coefficients with confidence intervals for publication tables
coef_table <- function(model, terms = NULL, term_labels = NULL,
                       vcov_mat = NULL, conf_level = 0.95,
                       outcome = NULL, model_label = NULL) {
  coef_summary <- as.data.frame(coef(summary(model)))

  if (is.null(vcov_mat)) {
    vcov_mat <- if (inherits(model, "lm")) {
      vcov_robust(model)
    } else {
      vcov(model)
    }
  }

  est <- if (inherits(model, "merMod")) lme4::fixef(model) else coef(model)
  se <- sqrt(diag(vcov_mat))
  term_names <- names(est)
  df_error <- if ("df" %in% names(coef_summary)) {
    coef_summary$df
  } else {
    rep(df.residual(model), length(est))
  }

  crit <- ifelse(
    is.finite(df_error),
    qt(1 - (1 - conf_level) / 2, df = df_error),
    qnorm(1 - (1 - conf_level) / 2)
  )
  statistic <- est / se
  p.value <- ifelse(
    is.finite(df_error),
    2 * pt(abs(statistic), df = df_error, lower.tail = FALSE),
    2 * pnorm(abs(statistic), lower.tail = FALSE)
  )

  out <- tibble(
    term = term_names,
    estimate = unname(est),
    std.error = unname(se),
    conf.low = estimate - crit * std.error,
    conf.high = estimate + crit * std.error,
    statistic = unname(statistic),
    df_error = unname(df_error),
    p.value = unname(p.value)
  )

  if (!is.null(terms)) {
    out <- out %>%
      filter(term %in% terms) %>%
      mutate(term = factor(term, levels = terms)) %>%
      arrange(term) %>%
      mutate(term = as.character(term))
  }

  if (!is.null(term_labels)) {
    out$label <- dplyr::recode(out$term, !!!term_labels)
  } else {
    out$label <- out$term
  }

  out %>%
    select(label, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, df_error, p.value) %>%
    rename(term = label) %>%
    mutate(
      outcome = outcome,
      model = model_label,
      .before = 1
    )
}

apa_p_value <- function(p) {
  case_when(
    is.na(p) ~ NA_character_,
    p < .001 ~ "< .001",
    TRUE ~ sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", round(p, 3)))
  )
}

apa_effect_table <- function(tbl, estimate_label = "Beta", ci_label = "95% CI for beta") {
  if (nrow(tbl) == 0) {
    out <- tibble(
      Outcome = character(),
      Model = character(),
      Effect = character(),
      estimate = character(),
      SE = character(),
      ci = character(),
      p = character()
    )
    names(out)[4] <- estimate_label
    names(out)[6] <- ci_label
    return(out)
  }

  out <- tbl %>%
    transmute(
      Outcome = outcome,
      Model = model,
      Effect = term,
      estimate = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
      SE = sprintf("%.2f", std.error),
      ci = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", conf.low, conf.high),
      p = apa_p_value(p.value)
    )

  names(out)[4] <- estimate_label
  names(out)[6] <- ci_label
  out
}

cor_effect_table <- function(data, x, y, outcome_label,
                             effect_label = "Bivariate correlation",
                             model_label = "Pearson correlation",
                             conf_level = 0.95) {
  pair_data <- data %>%
    select(all_of(c(x, y))) %>%
    filter(!if_any(everything(), is.na))

  test <- cor.test(pair_data[[x]], pair_data[[y]], conf.level = conf_level)

  tibble(
    Outcome = outcome_label,
    Model = model_label,
    Effect = effect_label,
    r = sprintf("%.2f", unname(test$estimate)),
    `95% CI for r` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", test$conf.int[1], test$conf.int[2]),
    p = apa_p_value(test$p.value)
  )
}

extract_effect_row <- function(tbl, outcome_name, term_name = NULL) {
  out <- tbl[tbl$outcome == outcome_name, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!is.null(term_name)) {
    out <- out[out$term == term_name, , drop = FALSE]
  }
  out[1, , drop = FALSE]
}

fmt_effect_estimate <- function(tbl, outcome_name, term_name = NULL, digits = 2) {
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), extract_effect_row(tbl, outcome_name, term_name)$estimate)
}

fmt_effect_ci <- function(tbl, outcome_name, term_name = NULL, digits = 2) {
  row <- extract_effect_row(tbl, outcome_name, term_name)
  sprintf(paste0("[%.", digits, "f, %.", digits, "f]"), row$conf.low, row$conf.high)
}

fmt_effect_p <- function(tbl, outcome_name, term_name = NULL) {
  apa_p_value(extract_effect_row(tbl, outcome_name, term_name)$p.value)
}
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

The sample includes 10,808 boys, 13,245 girls, 306 diverse/other, and 45 un-answered respondents, totaling 24,404 with an average age of 13.41 years. Respondents reported an average of 203.70 minutes per day on their smartphone, with 85.09 minutes specifically on SNS usage. In terms of well-being, 67.7% of the sample with non-missing PHQ-9 data (N = 24,216) scored in the minimal/none to mild range on depressive symptoms, whereas 18.9% were in the moderate range and 12.6% in the moderately severe to severe range. The mean satisfaction score was 5.50 (N = 24,396) on the 1-7 scale, with scores skewed to the left.

```{r Correlation}
make_cor_matrix <- function(data, vars, path) {
  df <- data %>%
    select(all_of(vars)) %>%
    mutate(
      dem_male    = as.integer(dem_gender == "male"),
      dem_female  = as.integer(dem_gender == "female"),
      across(where(is.factor), ~ as.numeric(.)),
      across(where(is.character), ~ as.numeric(as.factor(.)))
    ) %>%
    select(-dem_gender)

  cor_mat <- cor(df, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  p_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = ncol(df), ncol = ncol(df),
                  dimnames = list(names(df), names(df)))

  for (i in seq_along(df)) {
    for (j in seq_along(df)) {
      if (i == j) {
        p_mat[i, j] <- NA_real_
      } else {
        pair_data <- tibble(x = df[[i]], y = df[[j]]) %>%
          filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y))

        p_mat[i, j] <- if (nrow(pair_data) > 2) {
          suppressWarnings(cor.test(pair_data$x, pair_data$y)$p.value)
        } else {
          NA_real_
        }
      }
    }
  }

  format_cor <- function(r, p, diagonal = FALSE) {
    if (is.na(r)) return(NA_character_)
    cor_label <- sprintf("%.2f", round(r, 2))
    cor_label <- sub("^0\\.", ".", cor_label)
    cor_label <- sub("^-0\\.", "-.", cor_label)

    if (diagonal) {
      return(cor_label)
    }

    if (!is.na(p) && p < .05) {
      paste0(cor_label, "*")
    } else {
      cor_label
    }
  }

  mat <- matrix(
    nrow = ncol(df),
    ncol = ncol(df),
    dimnames = list(names(df), names(df))
  )

  for (i in seq_len(ncol(df))) {
    for (j in seq_len(ncol(df))) {
      mat[i, j] <- format_cor(cor_mat[i, j], p_mat[i, j], diagonal = i == j)
    }
  }

  mat <- as.data.frame(mat, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  write.csv(mat, path, row.names = TRUE)
  mat
}

cor_matrix_d_key  <- make_cor_matrix(
  d,
  key_vars_base,
  "results/cor_matrix_d_key.csv"
) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("variable") %>%
  filter(variable %in% key_vars_final) %>%
  select(variable, all_of(key_vars_final))
```

### Measurement Analysis

Our outcome variables of interest, the PHQ-9 item responses and the satisfaction responses, demonstrate good internal consistency with Cronbach's alpha of .85 and .84, respectively. 1-factor CFAs for the PHQ-9 and satisfaction item sets were also ran using the WLSMV estimator.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false"}

### **Question 1: Is young people's mental health deteriorating?**

```{r longitudinal-setup}
summary_year <- d %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise_stats() %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(as.character(year)))

summary_half_year <- d %>%
  group_by(year_half) %>%
  summarise_stats()

summary_quarter <- d %>%
  group_by(year_quarter) %>%
  summarise_stats()

summary_month_2025 <- d_2025 %>%
  group_by(year_month) %>%
  summarise_stats() %>%
  mutate(year_month = ymd(year_month)) %>%
  filter(n >= 50)

summary_month_covariates <- d %>%
  group_by(year_month) %>%
  summarise(
    prop_female = mean(dem_gender == "female", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

summary_month_all <- d %>%
  group_by(year_month) %>%
  summarise_stats() %>%
  left_join(summary_month_covariates, by = "year_month") %>%
  mutate(year_month = ymd(year_month)) %>%
  filter(n >= 50) %>%
  mutate(
      month     = factor(month(year_month)),
      time      = row_number(),
      post_ban  = if_else(year_month >= ban_date, 1, 0),
      time_post = if_else(post_ban == 1, time - min(time[post_ban == 1]) + 1L, 0L)
  )
```

#### Results

In the multilevel model, the share of variance attributable to school was 0.013 for depressive symptoms and 0.019 for satisfaction. The share of variance attributable to month was 0.0006 for depressive symptoms and 0.0005 for satisfaction. Neither well-being indicator showed a meaningful trend over the observed period. Depressive symptoms had a small, non-significant negative trend per month (b = −0.018, p = .082), whereas satisfaction had a near-zero positive trend (b = 0.001, p = .46). Within this Austrian sample and observation window, there is no clear evidence that well-being continued to deteriorate before the school phone ban.

#### Sensitivity to Unobserved Confounding (E-value)

The effect tables report standardized beta coefficients for comparability across models. The E-values are derived from the corresponding raw adjusted OLS models, evaluated for a 60-minute increase in SNS time, so that sensitivity to unobserved confounding remains interpretable in the original unit of minutes. Larger E-values indicate that stronger unmeasured confounding would be needed to explain away the observed association.

::: panel-tabset
## PHQ-9

The E-value of 1.52 (95% CI bound: 1.50) indicates that an unobserved confounder would need to be associated with both SNS use and depression symptoms by a factor of at least 1.52 on the risk ratio scale to explain away the observed effect. This suggests that the observed association is susceptible to a moderate level of unobserved confounding.

```{r question2-evalue-phq}

question2_phq_evalue_model_raw <- lm(phq9_score ~ mins_socnet + dem_income + dem_gender + dem_age + dem_liv_wi_bth_prnts + dem_own_room + dem_AUS + dem_siblings, data = d)

question2_evalue_phq <- EValue::evalues.OLS(
  est = coef(question2_phq_evalue_model_raw)[["mins_socnet"]],
  se = sqrt(diag(vcov_robust(question2_phq_evalue_model_raw)))[["mins_socnet"]],
  sd = sigma(question2_phq_evalue_model_raw),
  delta = 60
) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Estimate") %>%
  mutate(Outcome = "PHQ-9", .before = 1)

knitr::kable(question2_evalue_phq)
```

## Satisfaction

The E-value of 1.47 (95% CI bound: 1.45) indicates that an unobserved confounder would need to be associated with both SNS use and satisfaction levels by a factor of at least 1.47 on the risk ratio scale to explain away the observed effect. This suggests that the observed association is susceptible to a moderate level of unobserved confounding.

```{r question2-evalue-sat}

question2_sat_evalue_model_raw <- lm(sat_avg ~ mins_socnet + dem_income + dem_gender + dem_age +
dem_liv_wi_bth_prnts + dem_own_room + dem_AUS + dem_siblings, data = d)


question2_evalue_sat <- EValue::evalues.OLS(
  est = coef(question2_sat_evalue_model_raw)[["mins_socnet"]],
  se = sqrt(diag(vcov_robust(question2_sat_evalue_model_raw)))[["mins_socnet"]],
  sd = sigma(question2_sat_evalue_model_raw),
  delta = 60
) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Estimate") %>%
  mutate(Outcome = "Satisfaction", .before = 1)

question2_evalue <- bind_rows(question2_evalue_phq, question2_evalue_sat) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(., 2)))
write.csv(question2_evalue, "results/question2_evalues.csv", row.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(question2_evalue_sat)
```
:::

#### Results

SNS use had a positive correlation with depressive symptoms (r = .30) and a negative correlation with life satisfaction (r = –.29). Standardized OLS models controlling for covariates showed that greater SNS use predicted higher depressive symptoms and lower life satisfaction, with both effects statistically significant and exceeding the predefined minimum effect size threshold of \|β\| = .05. However, sensitivity analyses using E-values indicated that the observed effects could be explained away by an unmeasured confounder with a risk ratio of 1.52 for PHQ-9 and 1.47 for life satisfaction, both falling below the informal twofold threshold suggested by VanderWeele & Ding (2017). Accordingly, the observed effects appear moderately susceptible to unmeasured confounding.

```{r question2-correlation-summary}
    x = "mins_socnet",
    y = "phq9_score",
    outcome_label = "Depressive symptoms"
  ),
  cor_effect_table(
    d,
    x = "mins_socnet",
    y = "sat_avg",
    outcome_label = "Life satisfaction"
  )
)

knitr::kable(question2_correlations, align = "l")
```

### **Question 3: Are effects more negative for social networking sites than for instant messengers?**

::: panel-tabset
## Depressive Symptoms (PHQ-9)

The standardized coefficient for SNS minutes is higher than that for instant messaging, with the difference being statistically significant (p \< .001). Therefore, our data does support the question that SNSs are more "harmful" than messaging apps.

```{r}
question3_phq_sns_model_std <- lm(phq9_score_z ~ mins_socnet_z + dem_income_z + dem_gender + dem_age_z + dem_liv_wi_bth_prnts + dem_own_room + dem_AUS + dem_siblings_z, data = d)
question3_phq_messaging_model_std <- lm(phq9_score_z ~ mins_messenger_z + dem_income_z + dem_gender + dem_age_z + dem_liv_wi_bth_prnts + dem_own_room + dem_AUS + dem_siblings_z, data = d)

cat("\nSNS + Messenger:\n")
question3_phq_joint_model_std <- lm(phq9_score_z ~ mins_socnet_z + mins_messenger_z + dem_income_z + dem_gender + dem_age_z + dem_liv_wi_bth_prnts + dem_own_room + dem_AUS + dem_siblings_z,
  data = d)
model_output(question3_phq_joint_model_std)

linearHypothesis(question3_phq_joint_model_std, "mins_socnet_z = mins_messenger_z")

```

## Satisfaction

The standardized coefficient for SNS minutes is higher than that for instant messaging, with the difference being statistically significant (p \< .001). Therefore, our data does support the question that SNSs are more "harmful" than messaging apps.

:::

#### Results

SNS use had a stronger effect on both well-being outcomes compared to instant messaging use. For depressive symptoms (N = 20,287), the standardized coefficient for SNS time exceeded that for messaging time, and this difference was statistically significant (F(1, 20276) = 150, p \< .001). The same pattern held for satisfaction (N = 20,412), with a stronger association for SNS use than for instant messaging, F(1, 20401) = 179, p \< .001. These results indicate that SNS use has a stronger adverse relationship to well-being than instant messaging does.

#### Results

The SNS × age interaction term was statistically significant for both well-being outcomes in the analytic sample confined to ages 10 to 19. For depressive symptoms (N = 20,166), the negative interaction indicated that the effect of SNS use on depressive symptoms weakened with increasing age. In terms of life satisfaction (N = 20,291), the positive interaction similarly signaled that the negative relationship between SNS use and satisfaction weakened with age. Figure 6 below illustrates predicted slopes using the original age metric rather than standardized age values. Results show that the adverse effects of SNS use on well-being are stronger among younger adolescents.

```{r question4-main-effects-summary}
  )
)
```

#### Results

SNS use was associated with poorer well-being across all gender groups, but the relationship was significantly stronger for girls. For depressive symptoms (N = 20,287), the baseline effect among boys was significantly larger for girls, while the additional effect for adolescents identifying as diverse or other gender did not reach statistical significance. The same pattern held for satisfaction (N = 20,412), with a significant baseline effect among boys and a significant additional effect for girls, but no significant additional effect for diverse or other gender. The non-significant results for the diverse/other gender group should be interpreted cautiously, however, as this group was much smaller than the male and female subsamples.

### **Question 6: Do Smartphone school bans improve mental health?**

Austria implemented a nationwide school phone ban on May 1, 2025. To evaluate whether smartphone bans improve mental health, we use descriptive trend plots, an interrupted time series design based on aggregated monthly means, and individual-level pre-post regression models, including OLS and multilevel models. These analyses assess whether the ban was associated with changes in smartphone use, SNS use, PHQ-9 scores, and satisfaction. Multilevel models additionally account for clustering within schools and months. Multilevel modeling with random intercepts for school and month is treated as the primary analysis. The share of variance attributable to school was modest, ranging from .016 for PHQ-9 to .052 for smartphone use, whereas the share attributable to month was negligible, ranging from around .0005 to .002.

::: panel-tabset
```{r mlm-prepost-setup}
d_pp_full <- d %>%
  mutate(
    started_date = as.Date(STARTED),
    post_ban     = if_else(started_date >= ban_date, 1, 0)
  )

schools_both <- d_pp_full %>%
  group_by(school_name) %>%
  summarise(has_pre = any(post_ban == 0), has_post = any(post_ban == 1), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(has_pre & has_post, !is.na(school_name), school_name != "Unmatched")

d_ml <- d_pp_full %>%
  filter(school_name %in% schools_both$school_name)
```

## Pre-Post Visualization

```{r }
      panel,
      levels = c("Smartphone time", "SNS time", "Depressive Symptoms", "Satisfaction")
    )
  )

question6_axis_limits <- tibble(
  panel = factor(
    c("Smartphone time", "SNS time", "Depressive Symptoms", "Satisfaction"),
    levels = c("Smartphone time", "SNS time", "Depressive Symptoms", "Satisfaction")
  ),
  ymin = c(0, 0, 0, 3),
  ymax = c(360, 180, 10, 7)
)

question6_trend_data <- question6_trend_data %>%
  left_join(question6_axis_limits, by = "panel")

question6_year_breaks <- seq(
  as.Date("2023-01-01"),
  floor_date(max(summary_month_all$year_month), unit = "year"),
  by = "1 year"
)

question6_x_limits <- c(
  as.Date("2023-01-01"),
  ceiling_date(max(summary_month_all$year_month), unit = "month") - days(1)
)

ggplot(question6_trend_data, aes(x = year_month, y = value, group = 1)) +
  geom_blank(aes(y = ymin)) +
  geom_blank(aes(y = ymax)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = panel), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(color = panel), size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = vline_date, linetype = "dashed", color = "#B33A3A") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Smartphone time" = "#5F7386",
      "SNS time" = "#8EA1B3",
      "Depressive Symptoms" = "#B33A3A",
      "Satisfaction" = "#3C8D5A"
    ),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    limits = question6_x_limits,
    breaks = question6_year_breaks,
    labels = format(question6_year_breaks, "%Y"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Monthly mean"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    aspect.ratio = 0.9
  )
  
```

## Smartphone Multilevel Model

```{r mlm-prepost-smartphone}

cat("\nMonth as Random Effect\n")
question6_mlm_smartphone_model_month_re <- lmer(
  mins_smartphone ~ post_ban + dem_income + dem_gender + dem_age +
    dem_liv_wi_bth_prnts + dem_own_room + dem_AUS + dem_siblings +
    (1 | school_name) + (1 | month),
  data = d_ml, REML = TRUE
)
print_icc_components(question6_mlm_smartphone_model_month_re)
model_output(question6_mlm_smartphone_model_month_re)

```

:::

#### Results

Smartphone use faced a small but non-significant decline post-ban of 6.88 minutes (p = .071). The reduction in SNS use was also minor, at 4.31 minutes, and not statistically significant (p = .12). Depressive symptoms showed a non-significant post-ban shift (b = 0.0458, p = .70), and life satisfaction had a non-significant increase of 0.052 units on a 1-7 scale (p = .064).  These findings suggest that, when the analysis date is set to May 1st, the ban did not translate into reductions in smartphone or SNS use, nor improvements in well-being within the observation window captured by this dataset. 

```{r question6-main-effects-summary}
question6_effects_main <- bind_rows(
  coef_table(
    question6_mlm_smartphone_model_month_re,
    terms = "post_ban",
    term_labels = c(post_ban = "Post-ban indicator"),
    outcome = "Smartphone time",
    model_label = "Multilevel model"
  ),
  coef_table(
    question6_mlm_sns_model_month_re,
    terms = "post_ban",
    term_labels = c(post_ban = "Post-ban indicator"),
    outcome = "SNS time",
    model_label = "Multilevel model"
  ),
  coef_table(
    question6_mlm_phq_model_month_re,
    terms = "post_ban",
    term_labels = c(post_ban = "Post-ban indicator"),
    outcome = "Depressive symptoms",
    model_label = "Multilevel model"
  ),
  coef_table(
    question6_mlm_sat_model_month_re,
    terms = "post_ban",
    term_labels = c(post_ban = "Post-ban indicator"),
    outcome = "Satisfaction",
    model_label = "Multilevel model"
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  apa_effect_table(
    question6_effects_main,
    estimate_label = "b",
    ci_label = "95% CI for b"
  ),
  align = "l"
)
```

#### Exploratory Analysis: July 1, 2025 Cutoff

::: panel-tabset
```{r mlm-prepost-setup-july}
d_pp_full_july <- d %>%
  mutate(
    started_date = as.Date(STARTED),
    post_july    = if_else(started_date >= question6_explore_date, 1, 0)
  )

schools_both_july <- d_pp_full_july %>%
  group_by(school_name) %>%
  summarise(has_pre = any(post_july == 0), has_post = any(post_july == 1), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(has_pre & has_post, !is.na(school_name), school_name != "Unmatched")

d_ml_july <- d_pp_full_july %>%
  filter(school_name %in% schools_both_july$school_name)
```

:::

#### Results

We re-conducted the pre-post analysis using July 1, instead of May 1, as the cut-off, given the Graz school shooting on June 10, 2025, which may have affected students’ well-being and confounded the immediate post-ban outcomes. This alternative cutoff yielded several shifts in the results. Smartphone use showed a significant, albeit small, decline. Life satisfaction also saw a modest but statistically significant increase on the 1-7 scale. The trend for SNS use and depressive symptoms remained largely unchanged. In sum, the post-July 1 analysis revealed minor but statistically significant reductions in smartphone use and modest improvements in life satisfaction, but no significant changes in SNS use or depressive symptoms.

```{r question6-july-effects-summary}
  ),
```
